results.text: Ordering is not guaranteed for events transported through the Amazon SQS standard queues. Any consumer that requires ordering must sort events using the event `occurred_at` field. | When: Saturday, August 1, 2026, as an ongoing consequence and consumer-handling rule of the selected transport design | Involving: Widget-event consumers, especially any consumer whose processing logic requires ordered events; event producers must provide the event `occurred_at` field for that consumer-side sorting strategy | The design explicitly accepts the consequence that SQS standard queues do not guarantee ordering. Consumers that need ordering remain responsible for reconstructing order by sorting on `occurred_at`; ordering is not provided by the queue transport itself.

results.text: Every widget queue must have a dead-letter queue. Messages must move to the DLQ after 5 receives, configured as `maxReceiveCount: 5`. The visibility timeout must be `90 seconds` on all widget queues. | When: Saturday, August 1, 2026, as a requirement established by the event-transport specification; the requirements are ongoing for all widget queues | Involving: Widget-event producers and consumers, Amazon SQS, and the operators responsible for configuring and monitoring the queues | The dead-letter-queue requirement provides a defined failure path for messages that cannot be successfully processed after repeated receives. The exact threshold, `maxReceiveCount: 5`, makes failure handling actionable and deterministic. The `90 seconds` visibility timeout controls how long a received message remains hidden from other consumers before it can be delivered again.

results.text: Consumers must be idempotent. Because Amazon SQS standard queues deliver messages at least once, duplicate delivery is expected behavior and must not be treated as an error. | When: Saturday, August 1, 2026, as an ongoing consumer-processing requirement | Involving: All widget-event consumers and the Amazon SQS standard-queue delivery system | At-least-once delivery means the same message can be delivered more than once. Idempotent consumer behavior is therefore an acceptance criterion required to prevent duplicate delivery from causing incorrect repeated side effects or processing failures. Duplicate delivery is explicitly expected behavior, not an error.
